config.title: conic-gradient

intro.title: conic-gradient
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a colorful pie chart using CSS conic gradients. You will learn how to create smooth color transitions around a circle, starting from a single point. The core concept is the conic-gradient() function, which allows you to define colors at specific angles. You will work with CSS properties like background-image and border-radius to style your chart. By the end, you'll be able to create radial color patterns for visual elements on a webpage.
intro.usecase: Conic gradients are commonly used in modern UI design to create circular progress indicators, pie charts, and color wheels in dashboards and data visualization tools. You'll see them in fitness apps showing activity rings, financial apps displaying budget allocations, or analytics platforms visualizing percentage distributions. Developers implement conic gradients for loading spinners, rating displays, and circular menus that require smooth color transitions around a center point. This technique is essential for creating visually engaging circular interfaces without complex image assets.

objectives: Construct a basic conic-gradient with multiple color stops
Configure the starting angle of a conic-gradient
Apply conic-gradient to create a color wheel
Manipulate color distribution using percentage values
Integrate conic-gradient with other CSS properties for visual effects
Control gradient transitions between color stops

steps.title: Create a basic HTML structure for the conic-gradient lesson
steps.instruction: Create an HTML file with a basic structure including a container div and several child divs that will be styled with conic gradients.
steps.hint: Start with the standard HTML5 doctype and structure. Inside the body, create a main container div with class 'gradient-container', then add three child divs with classes 'gradient-circle', 'gradient-pie', and 'gradient-wheel'.

    <title>Conic Gradient Lesson</title>
</head>
<body>

</body>

steps.title: Create a repeating-conic-gradient pattern
steps.instruction: Add a new CSS rule for a class named 'repeating-pattern' that applies a repeating-conic-gradient with alternating black and white stripes (black 0deg 15deg, white 15deg 30deg) to create a striped pattern.
steps.hint: Use the repeating-conic-gradient() function with color stops defined by degree ranges. The pattern will repeat automatically to fill the element.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new CSS rule is added that creates a repeating striped pattern using alternating black and white sections.
successCriteria: Contains color stops: black 0deg 15deg and white 15deg 30deg
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your repeating-conic-gradient has both color stops with degree ranges.
steps.feedbackWrong: The pattern wasn't created correctly. Make sure to use repeating-conic-gradient() with the specified color stops.

steps.title: Combine conic-gradient with other CSS properties
steps.instruction: In the .gradient-box CSS rule, add border-radius: 50% to make the element circular.
steps.hint: Add the border-radius property inside the existing .gradient-box selector to create a perfect circle.
steps.expectedOutcome: The gradient box becomes a perfect circle with a conic gradient color wheel effect.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added border-radius: 50% to the .gradient-box rule.
steps.feedbackWrong: The border-radius property is missing or incorrect. Add border-radius: 50% to the .gradient-box selector.

steps.title: Create a pie chart using conic-gradient

steps.hint: Use conic-gradient with color stops at specific percentages to create distinct segments. For example, red 0% 30%, blue 30% 70%, green 70% 100%.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new .pie-chart CSS rule is added that creates a pie chart visualization using conic-gradient with percentage-based color stops.
successCriteria: The .pie-chart rule includes width, height, conic-gradient with at least two color stops using percentages, and border-radius to make it circular.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your conic-gradient includes specific percentage values for color stops (e.g., red 0% 30%, blue 30% 70%) and the border-radius property to make it circular.
